children.name: Self-Driving Laboratories
children.blurb: Self-driving laboratories are lab systems that close the loop between experiment design, robotic execution, measurement, and model update.

children.name: Digital Twins for Experiments
children.blurb: Digital twins for experiments are computational models of a physical experiment, instrument, or sample that stay synchronized with real data.

children.name: Instrument and Sensor Data
children.blurb: Instrument and sensor data is the stream of measurements that laboratory instruments and sensors produce, together with the context that makes those measurements meaningful.

children.name: Optimising Lab Protocols
children.blurb: Optimising lab protocols covers the design, scheduling, and revision of experimental procedures so that they use less time, reagent, and labour while producing more reliable results.

children.name: Forecasting Lab Supplies
children.blurb: Forecasting lab supplies covers the prediction of demand for reagents, consumables, and small equipment in a laboratory, from pipette tips and culture plates to antibodies and solvents.

sections.body: Laboratory automation and simulation covers the machinery and software that run experiments with less human hands-on time, and the models that mirror a physical lab in software. In practice, AI here schedules robotic liquid handlers, reads instrument output, adjusts parameters between runs, and predicts when reagents will run out. Self-driving labs close the loop, where a model proposes a condition, a robot runs it, and the result feeds the next proposal. Digital twins hold a live copy of an experiment or a whole facility so that changes can be tried in simulation first. The work is less about discovery in the abstract and more about throughput, reproducibility and keeping expensive instruments busy.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Closed-loop systems exist and run real chemistry and biology, though most operate inside narrow, well-instrumented domains where the robot can actually touch the sample. Data quality remains the binding constraint, because instrument files arrive in inconsistent formats and calibration drifts quietly. Digital twins are useful for planning and fault detection but rarely match a physical system closely enough to replace a real run. Protocol optimisation has produced solid gains in scheduling and reagent use, and supply forecasting is mostly a demand and lead-time problem that standard methods already handle well. The honest limit is that autonomy is bounded by what the hardware can sense and move, not by the models.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: Start with Self-Driving Laboratories for the closed-loop idea and the hardware that makes it possible, then read Digital Twins for Experiments for the simulation side that lets a lab test changes without consuming material. Instrument and Sensor Data is the foundation page, covering how readings are captured, cleaned and fed into everything else, and it is the one to read first if the data pipeline is your concern. Optimising Lab Protocols shows how those inputs turn into better schedules and conditions, while Forecasting Lab Supplies handles the inventory and ordering layer that keeps a running lab from stalling. Read together, the five pages trace a single arc from raw signal to autonomous decision, and each stands alone for readers who only need one part of that chain.
